case: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of dark brown urine and puffiness around his eyes for 2 days. Three weeks ago he had crusted, honey-colored sores around his nose and mouth that healed without treatment. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 138/90 mm Hg (95th percentile for age and height, about 110/74). Physical examination shows periorbital edema and 1+ pitting edema of the ankles. Urinalysis shows cola-colored urine with 3+ blood and 2+ protein. Laboratory studies show serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (0.3 to 0.7), C3 38 mg/dL (90 to 180), C4 24 mg/dL (10 to 40), and an elevated anti-DNase B titer. Diagnosis: poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: Plasma renin activity and atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) are measured. Which of the following sets of findings is most likely?
options: Increased renin and decreased atrial natriuretic peptide
Increased renin and increased atrial natriuretic peptide
Decreased renin and increased atrial natriuretic peptide
Decreased renin and decreased atrial natriuretic peptide
approach: Inflamed glomeruli filter less, so the kidney retains sodium and water and the extracellular volume expands.
Expanded volume and high pressure at the afferent arteriole suppress renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells.
Stretched atria release ANP, so this is a high-volume, low-renin form of hypertension.
questions.why: In acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis the GFR falls and the tubules keep reabsorbing sodium, so salt and water are retained. The hypertension and edema come from this volume expansion. Higher perfusion pressure at the juxtaglomerular cells and less sympathetic drive turn renin down, so renin and aldosterone are low. Atrial stretch raises ANP, which would normally promote natriuresis, but the injured kidney responds poorly to it.
whyNot: This pattern fits volume depletion or renal artery stenosis, where low perfusion pressure drives renin up and the atria are underfilled.
Renin and ANP rarely rise together. High renin with high ANP would need low renal perfusion and atrial stretch at the same time, as in some heart failure states.
Correct.
Low ANP means the atria are not stretched. This child is volume expanded, with edema and hypertension.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
options: Urine protein under 3.5 g/day with oliguria
Serum albumin under 2.5 g/dL with hyperlipidemia
Oval fat bodies and fatty casts in the urine
Selective albuminuria with normal urine output
approach: Hematuria, hypertension, edema, and a rising creatinine after an infection point to a nephritic syndrome.
Nephritic disease comes from inflammation that injures the capillary wall and lowers GFR, so urine output falls and proteinuria is usually modest.
Pick the finding that belongs to the nephritic picture and reject the features of nephrotic syndrome.
questions.why: Nephritic syndrome is driven by glomerular inflammation. Red cells leak into the urine, GFR falls, and salt and water retention cause hypertension, oliguria, and azotemia. Proteinuria is present but usually below 3.5 g/day. Nephrotic syndrome is defined by proteinuria above 3.5 g/day with hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria.
whyNot: Correct.
Severe hypoalbuminemia (reference 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL) with hyperlipidemia defines nephrotic syndrome. Postinfectious glomerulonephritis only rarely reaches nephrotic-range protein loss.
Oval fat bodies and fatty casts come from heavy lipoprotein loss in nephrotic syndrome.
Selective albuminuria with preserved output is typical of minimal change disease in a child. It does not fit hematuria, hypertension, and azotemia.

questions.stem: Culture of the skin lesions 3 weeks ago would most likely have grown which of the following organisms?
options: Catalase-positive, coagulase-positive cocci in clusters
Beta-hemolytic, bacitracin-resistant, CAMP-positive cocci
Alpha-hemolytic, optochin-sensitive lancet-shaped diplococci
Beta-hemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive cocci in chains
approach: Nephritis about 3 weeks after impetigo, with low C3 and a raised anti-DNase B titer, means a preceding infection with a nephritogenic strain of group A streptococcus.
Identify group A streptococcus in the laboratory: gram-positive cocci in chains, catalase negative, beta-hemolytic, and bacitracin sensitive.
questions.why: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis follows infection with certain nephritogenic strains of Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). After pharyngitis the latent period is about 1 to 2 weeks; after skin infection it is about 3 to 6 weeks. Group A streptococci are catalase-negative, beta-hemolytic cocci in chains that are sensitive to bacitracin and PYR positive. After skin infection the antistreptolysin O titer often stays low, so anti-DNase B is the better marker.
whyNot: Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause of impetigo, but it does not cause poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Staphylococcal infection is linked to a different, IgA-dominant glomerulonephritis that occurs during active infection.
This describes Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), which causes neonatal sepsis and meningitis and is not a cause of postinfectious nephritis after impetigo.
This describes Streptococcus pneumoniae, which causes pneumonia, otitis, and meningitis and does not cause impetigo.
Correct.

questions.stem: If a renal biopsy were performed, which of the following findings on immunofluorescence and electron microscopy would most likely be seen?
options: Linear IgG along the basement membrane, no dense deposits
Granular IgG and C3 with subepithelial humps
Mesangial IgA with mesangial dense deposits
Granular IgG, C3, and C1q with subendothelial deposits
approach: Low C3 with normal C4 after a streptococcal infection points to immune complex disease that activates complement mainly through the alternative pathway.
Immune complexes give a granular (lumpy-bumpy) pattern of IgG and C3.
In this disease the large deposits sit on the outer side of the basement membrane, under the podocytes.
questions.why: Streptococcal antigens such as SpeB and nephritis-associated plasmin receptor deposit in the glomerulus and bind antibody, forming immune complexes in place and from the circulation. Immunofluorescence shows granular IgG and C3 along capillary walls and in the mesangium. Electron microscopy shows the classic subepithelial humps. Complement activation lowers serum C3, which returns to normal within about 6 to 8 weeks.
whyNot: Linear IgG with no deposits is anti-GBM disease, where antibodies bind the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen directly.
Correct.
Mesangial IgA deposits define IgA nephropathy and IgA vasculitis, which have normal complement levels.
Full-house granular staining with C1q and subendothelial wire-loop deposits suggests lupus nephritis, which lowers both C3 and C4.

dx: IgA nephropathy with gross hematuria after a viral pharyngitis
case: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician because of red-brown urine that began yesterday, 1 day after the onset of a sore throat and runny nose. He had a similar episode of dark urine during a cold 1 year ago that cleared within a week. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pharyngeal erythema and no edema. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood, 1+ protein, and dysmorphic red blood cells. Serum creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Serum C3 and C4 concentrations are within the reference ranges. A renal biopsy shows mesangial proliferation with dominant mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence. Diagnosis: IgA nephropathy.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the immunologic mechanism of this patient's glomerular injury?
options: Deposition of circulating IgA1-containing immune complexes
Antibodies binding the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
ANCA-mediated neutrophil activation without immune deposits
Cytokine release from T cells injuring podocytes
approach: Granular mesangial IgA deposits mean antigen-antibody complexes are lodging in the glomerulus.
Tissue injury from immune complexes that activate complement and recruit inflammatory cells is type III hypersensitivity.
Match the mechanism to IgA nephropathy and reject type II and pauci-immune disease.
questions.why: IgA nephropathy is a type III immune complex disease. Patients make IgA1 with too little galactose in its hinge region. Autoantibodies of the IgG or IgA class bind this abnormal IgA1, and the complexes deposit in the mesangium. They stimulate mesangial cells to proliferate and activate complement through the alternative and lectin pathways. Mucosal infections boost IgA1 production, which is why flares follow colds.
whyNot: Correct.
Antibody to a fixed antigen in the basement membrane is type II hypersensitivity. It is the mechanism of anti-GBM disease and gives linear IgG staining.
ANCA vasculitis is pauci-immune, with little or no immunoglobulin in the glomerulus. This biopsy shows strong IgA deposits.
T cell cytokine injury to podocytes is the proposed mechanism of minimal change disease, which causes nephrotic syndrome with no immune deposits.

questions.stem: Urine protein electrophoresis is performed on a 24-hour collection. Which of the following patterns is most likely?
options: Mostly monoclonal free light chains
Mostly beta-2 microglobulin and lysozyme
Mostly uromodulin from the thick ascending limb
Mostly albumin
approach: Dysmorphic red cells show that the leak is in the glomerulus.
A damaged filtration barrier lets through plasma proteins that are normally held back, and albumin is the most plentiful of these.
Separate this glomerular pattern from overflow and tubular patterns.
questions.why: Proteinuria has three main sources. In glomerular proteinuria a damaged barrier lets albumin and sometimes larger proteins through, so albumin dominates. In overflow proteinuria small proteins such as free light chains are made in excess and swamp tubular reabsorption. In tubular proteinuria the barrier is intact, but the proximal tubule fails to take back the small proteins that are normally filtered.
whyNot: A monoclonal light chain peak is overflow proteinuria from a plasma cell disorder such as multiple myeloma.
Excess small proteins such as beta-2 microglobulin and lysozyme with little albumin is tubular proteinuria, seen in Fanconi syndrome and tubulointerstitial disease.
Uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein) is secreted by the thick ascending limb and is the main protein in normal urine. It forms the matrix of casts but does not cause disease-level proteinuria.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following other glomerular diseases also characteristically presents with normal serum complement concentrations?
options: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
Anti-GBM disease
Diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
approach: Complement falls when immune complexes in or around the glomerulus activate it faster than the liver can replace it.
Sort the options into diseases that consume complement and diseases that do not.
Anti-GBM antibody binds a fixed antigen, and serum complement stays normal.
questions.why: Serum complement helps narrow the cause of nephritis. Low complement points to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (low C3), membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (low C3), and lupus nephritis (low C3 and C4). Normal complement points to IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease, and ANCA-associated vasculitis. In anti-GBM disease complement is activated locally at the basement membrane, but not enough to lower serum levels.
whyNot: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis lowers C3 through alternative pathway activation, with recovery over about 6 to 8 weeks.
Correct.
Lupus nephritis consumes complement through the classical pathway, so both C3 and C4 are low during active disease.
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis typically lowers C3, from immune complexes or from C3 nephritic factor.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of this patient's presentation most strongly favors IgA nephropathy over poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
options: Red blood cell casts in the urine sediment
Pharyngitis as the preceding infection
Hematuria within a day of the sore throat
Dysmorphic red cells on urine microscopy
approach: Both diseases can follow an upper respiratory infection and both cause glomerular hematuria.
The timing differs: IgA nephropathy flares during or within a few days of the infection, while poststreptococcal disease follows after a latent period of weeks.
Choose the feature that one disease has and the other does not.
questions.why: In IgA nephropathy, gross hematuria starts during or within 1 to 3 days of a mucosal infection, so it is called synpharyngitic. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis appears about 1 to 2 weeks after pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks after impetigo, because antibody must form and immune complexes must build up first. Complement also separates them: normal in IgA nephropathy, low C3 in poststreptococcal disease. IgA nephropathy often recurs, while poststreptococcal disease rarely does.
whyNot: Red cell casts mark glomerular bleeding in any glomerulonephritis, so they appear in both diseases.
Pharyngitis precedes both diseases. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis can also follow skin infection.
Correct.
Dysmorphic red cells show that blood passed through a glomerulus. They are present in both diseases.

case: A 27-year-old man who smokes cigarettes is brought to the emergency department because of coughing up blood for 1 week and reduced urine output with dark urine for 3 days. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 150/94 mm Hg. Crackles are heard over both lung fields. A chest x-ray shows bilateral alveolar infiltrates. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), urea nitrogen 62 mg/dL (7 to 20), and creatinine 4.6 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Urinalysis shows 3+ blood, 2+ protein, and red blood cell casts. Serum anti-GBM antibodies are positive and ANCA is negative. A renal biopsy shows crescents in 80% of glomeruli with linear IgG along the basement membranes. Diagnosis: anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome).

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the lesions seen in most of his glomeruli on light microscopy?
options: Nodules of mesangial matrix with hyaline material
Proliferating mesangial cells with duplication of the basement membrane
Segmental sclerosis of the capillary tuft with adhesion to Bowman capsule
Parietal epithelial cells, macrophages, and fibrin in Bowman space
approach: Crescents in most glomeruli define rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis.
Severe injury tears the glomerular capillary wall, and fibrin and inflammatory cells pour into Bowman space.
Fibrin and cytokines drive parietal epithelial cells to proliferate, and macrophages join them to form the crescent.
questions.why: A crescent forms when severe injury ruptures the glomerular capillary wall. Fibrinogen leaks into Bowman space and becomes fibrin. Fibrin and inflammatory cytokines make the parietal epithelial cells proliferate, and monocytes and macrophages move in, so the crescent compresses the tuft. Untreated cellular crescents become fibrous scars, which is why rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis can cause renal failure within weeks.
whyNot: Nodular mesangial matrix (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules) is the lesion of diabetic nephropathy.
Mesangial proliferation with a split basement membrane is membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
Segmental sclerosis with adhesions is focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, a podocyte disease that causes nephrotic syndrome.
Correct.

topics: Crescent formation in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of tissue injury in this patient?
options: Type III, with granular deposits of circulating immune complexes
Type II, with antibody against a fixed tissue antigen
Type IV, with sensitized T cells releasing cytokines
Type I, with IgE-triggered mast cell degranulation
approach: Linear IgG along the basement membrane means antibody is binding an antigen built into the membrane itself.
Antibody against a fixed tissue antigen, followed by complement activation and neutrophil injury, is type II hypersensitivity.
The same antigen is present in alveolar basement membranes, which explains the lung hemorrhage.
questions.why: In anti-GBM disease, IgG autoantibodies bind the noncollagenous (NC1) domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. Because the antigen is spread evenly along the membrane, immunofluorescence shows a smooth linear pattern. The bound antibody activates complement and recruits neutrophils and macrophages, which tear the capillary wall. Alveolar basement membranes carry the same antigen. Smoking and other lung injury expose it, and pulmonary hemorrhage results.
whyNot: Immune complexes give granular deposits, as in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and lupus nephritis.
Correct.
Delayed T cell injury is seen in contact dermatitis and tuberculin reactions and does not produce linear IgG staining.
IgE-mediated reactions cause anaphylaxis, urticaria, and asthma. They do not cause glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: The target of his antibodies lies in the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, encoded by COL4A3. A heterozygous loss-of-function mutation in this gene in another person is most likely to cause which of the following?
options: Isolated hematuria with a thin basement membrane
Blue sclerae with fractures after minor trauma
Hyperextensible skin with widened atrophic scars
Spontaneous rupture of large arteries and colon
approach: Type IV collagen forms the sheet-like network of basement membranes, and the alpha-3, alpha-4, and alpha-5 chains make the mature glomerular basement membrane.
One normal COL4A3 allele still makes some network, so a heterozygous defect gives a thin but working membrane.
The result is persistent microscopic hematuria, usually with normal kidney function.
questions.why: The mature glomerular basement membrane is built from a network of alpha-3, alpha-4, and alpha-5 chains of type IV collagen. Mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4 on both alleles, or in X-linked COL4A5, cause Alport syndrome with a split, laminated membrane. A heterozygous COL4A3 or COL4A4 mutation causes thin basement membrane disease, with persistent microscopic hematuria and usually a benign course, though some carriers later develop proteinuria and loss of function.
whyNot: Correct.
Blue sclerae and fragile bones are osteogenesis imperfecta, most often from COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutations in type I collagen.
Hyperextensible skin and wide atrophic scars are classic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, most often from type V collagen mutations (COL5A1 or COL5A2).
Arterial and bowel rupture are vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, from COL3A1 mutations in type III collagen.

questions.stem: Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: pH 7.42 (7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 16 mm Hg (35 to 45), PaO2 56 mm Hg (75 to 100), and HCO3- 10 mEq/L (22 to 28). Serum sodium is 136 mEq/L and chloride is 104 mEq/L. Which of the following best describes his acid-base status?
options: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Metabolic acidosis with a concurrent respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis with a concurrent respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis with appropriate renal compensation
approach: The bicarbonate of 10 mEq/L and the anion gap of 22 (136 minus 104 minus 10) show an anion gap metabolic acidosis from renal failure.
Winters formula predicts PaCO2 = 1.5 x 10 + 8 = 23, give or take 2, so 21 to 25 mm Hg.
His PaCO2 of 16 is lower than predicted, so a second, respiratory alkalosis is present, driven here by hypoxemia from alveolar hemorrhage.
questions.why: Renal failure retains acids such as sulfate and phosphate, which lowers bicarbonate and raises the anion gap. Winters formula gives the PaCO2 expected from respiratory compensation alone. A PaCO2 below that range means the patient is breathing off more CO2 than compensation explains, which is a concurrent respiratory alkalosis. His hypoxemia from pulmonary hemorrhage drives this extra ventilation. A normal pH with clearly abnormal PaCO2 and bicarbonate is a strong clue to a mixed disorder.
whyNot: Appropriate compensation would put PaCO2 at about 21 to 25 mm Hg. His PaCO2 of 16 is too low.
A concurrent respiratory acidosis would leave PaCO2 above the predicted range, and the pH would be well below 7.35.
Correct.

Renal compensation for chronic respiratory alkalosis rarely lowers bicarbonate below about 12 to 15 mEq/L, and his illness is too recent for full compensation. The high anion gap also shows a separate metabolic acidosis.

dx: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis with crescentic glomerulonephritis
case: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of nasal crusting, bloody nasal discharge, and sinus pain for 2 months, and cough with blood-streaked sputum for 2 weeks. Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg. Examination shows ulcerated, crusted nasal mucosa. A chest x-ray shows several cavitating nodules. Serum creatinine is 3.2 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1); it was 0.9 mg/dL 4 months ago. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood and 2+ protein. Serum C3 and C4 concentrations are within the reference ranges. PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) is positive at a high titer. A renal biopsy shows necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis. Diagnosis: granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

questions.stem: Before the antibody results were available, multiple myeloma was considered as a cause of her renal failure. Which of the following urine findings would have most strongly suggested overflow proteinuria from that disorder?
options: Albumin accounting for most of the protein in the urine
Protein detected by sulfosalicylic acid but not dipstick
Protein detected by dipstick but not by sulfosalicylic acid
Uromodulin as the main protein in the urine
approach: In myeloma, plasma cells make excess free light chains that are small enough to be filtered and overwhelm proximal tubular reabsorption.
Urine dipsticks react mainly with albumin and miss light chains, while sulfosalicylic acid precipitates all proteins.
A positive sulfosalicylic acid test with a negative dipstick points to a non-albumin protein such as Bence Jones protein.
questions.why: Overflow proteinuria happens when the plasma holds too much of a small, freely filtered protein. In multiple myeloma, free light chains (Bence Jones protein) are filtered faster than the proximal tubule can take them back, so they appear in the urine. The dipstick pad is sensitive to albumin and poorly detects light chains. Sulfosalicylic acid precipitates any protein, so a gap between the two tests suggests light chains. Small tubular proteins can give the same gap, so urine electrophoresis and immunofixation are used to confirm a monoclonal light chain.
whyNot: Albumin-dominant proteinuria is glomerular. It fits her glomerulonephritis and argues against light chain overflow.
Correct.
A positive dipstick with a negative sulfosalicylic acid test is the reverse pattern. It suggests a false-positive dipstick, as in highly alkaline urine, and does not point to light chains.
Uromodulin is the main protein of normal urine, secreted by the thick ascending limb, and does not point to any disease.

questions.stem: Immunofluorescence microscopy of the biopsy specimen is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane
Granular IgG and C3 along capillary walls
Little or no immunoglobulin or complement
Dominant IgA deposits in the mesangium
approach: Crescentic glomerulonephritis is sorted into three groups by immunofluorescence: linear, granular, and pauci-immune.
Positive ANCA with normal complement places her in the pauci-immune group.
In ANCA disease, neutrophils activated by the antibodies damage vessels without leaving immune deposits.
questions.why: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis has three immunologic types. Anti-GBM disease shows linear IgG. Immune complex disease, such as lupus or postinfectious glomerulonephritis, shows granular deposits. Pauci-immune disease shows little or no immunoglobulin or complement and is usually ANCA positive. In granulomatosis with polyangiitis, ANCA binds proteinase 3 on primed neutrophils and makes them release enzymes and reactive oxygen species into the vessel wall. This damage leaves no immune deposits behind.
whyNot: Linear IgG is anti-GBM disease. She is ANCA positive and has upper airway disease, which fits granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Granular IgG and C3 indicate immune complex disease, which usually lowers complement. Her complement is normal.
Correct.
Mesangial IgA is IgA nephropathy or IgA vasculitis, which do not cause cavitating lung nodules or a positive PR3-ANCA.

questions.stem: Microscopic examination of her urine sediment is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Dysmorphic erythrocytes and red blood cell casts
Leukocytes and white blood cell casts with bacteria
Renal tubular cells and muddy brown granular casts
Broad waxy casts in a bland sediment
approach: Necrotizing glomerulonephritis breaks glomerular capillaries, and red cells enter the tubules.
Red cells squeezed through the capillary wall become misshapen, and red cells trapped in uromodulin within the tubule form casts.
Red cell casts place the bleeding in the glomerulus.
questions.why: Casts form in the tubules when uromodulin gels and traps whatever is in the lumen, so a cast shows where in the nephron the problem started. Red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells mean bleeding from inflamed glomeruli. White cell casts point to pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis. Muddy brown granular casts point to acute tubular necrosis. Fatty casts point to nephrotic syndrome, and waxy casts point to advanced chronic kidney disease.
whyNot: Correct.
White cell casts with bacteria indicate pyelonephritis, an infection of the tubules and interstitium.
Muddy brown granular casts and shed tubular cells indicate acute tubular necrosis, such as after ischemia or toxins.
Broad waxy casts form in dilated, slow-flowing tubules of advanced chronic kidney disease. Her decline happened over weeks.

topics: Urinary casts and what they localize

questions.stem: Which of the following findings best distinguishes her disease from microscopic polyangiitis?
options: Necrotizing glomerulonephritis with crescents
Palpable purpura of the lower legs
Microaneurysms of the renal arteries on angiography
Granulomatous inflammation of the airways
approach: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis are both ANCA-associated small vessel vasculitides that cause pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis.
They differ in that granulomatosis with polyangiitis forms necrotizing granulomas in the upper and lower respiratory tract and is usually PR3-ANCA positive.
Microscopic polyangiitis has no granulomas and is usually MPO-ANCA positive.
questions.why: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis has a classic triad of necrotizing granulomas of the upper airway (sinusitis, nasal ulcers, saddle nose), lung disease (nodules that may cavitate), and necrotizing glomerulonephritis. It is most often PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) positive. Microscopic polyangiitis causes the same kind of glomerulonephritis and lung capillaritis but no granulomas, and it is usually MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) positive. Polyarteritis nodosa affects medium arteries, spares glomeruli, and is ANCA negative.
whyNot: Both ANCA vasculitides cause necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis, so this does not separate them.
Palpable purpura from small vessel vasculitis of the skin can occur in both diseases.
Renal artery microaneurysms are a feature of polyarteritis nodosa, a medium vessel vasculitis that spares the glomeruli.
Correct.

case: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of swelling of her legs, painful joints, and a facial rash for 3 weeks. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 158/98 mm Hg. Examination shows an erythematous rash over the cheeks and nasal bridge that spares the nasolabial folds, tender swollen wrists, and 2+ pitting edema of the legs. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL (12 to 16), creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), and a positive antinuclear antibody test at 1:1280. Urine protein excretion is 2.4 g/24 h. A renal biopsy shows endocapillary proliferation in more than half of the glomeruli, wire-loop thickening of capillary walls, and granular IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q deposits. Diagnosis: diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis.

questions.stem: Four years later, after treatment, she has new swelling of her legs. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, serum albumin is 2.2 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5), and urine protein excretion is 7.5 g/24 h. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein, no blood, and no red blood cell casts. A repeat renal biopsy is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Mesangial hypercellularity with mesangial deposits only
Global sclerosis of more than 90 percent of glomeruli
Subepithelial deposits with basement membrane spikes
Subendothelial wire-loop deposits with endocapillary proliferation
approach: Heavy proteinuria with low albumin, edema, and no blood or casts in the urine is a nephrotic picture.
In lupus, the class that gives a nephrotic picture with a quiet sediment is membranous lupus nephritis (class V).
Membranous disease places immune deposits under the podocytes, and new basement membrane grows up around them as spikes.
questions.why: Lupus nephritis is classified by where the immune deposits sit and how much the glomeruli proliferate. Subendothelial deposits with proliferation (classes III and IV) give a nephritic picture with hematuria and red cell casts. Subepithelial deposits (class V, membranous lupus nephritis) injure podocytes and give nephrotic syndrome with little hematuria, like primary membranous nephropathy. A patient can move from one class to another over time, so a change in the urine picture is a reason to repeat the biopsy.
whyNot: Mesangial lupus nephritis (class II) usually causes mild hematuria or low-grade proteinuria, not nephrotic syndrome.
Advanced sclerosing lupus nephritis (class VI) means most glomeruli are scarred, so GFR would be markedly reduced. Her creatinine is normal.
Correct.
Active diffuse proliferative disease would give hematuria and red cell casts. Her sediment is bland.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of serum findings is most likely during this flare?
options: Low C3, low C4, high anti-dsDNA
Low C3, normal C4, high anti-dsDNA
Normal C3, normal C4, high anti-dsDNA
Normal C3, low C4, normal anti-dsDNA
approach: Full-house granular deposits with C1q mean immune complexes are activating complement through the classical pathway.
Classical pathway activation uses up C1, C4, and C2 before C3, so both C4 and C3 fall.
Anti-dsDNA antibodies help form these complexes, and their titer rises with active nephritis.
questions.why: Lupus nephritis is a type III immune complex disease. Complexes of anti-dsDNA and nuclear antigens deposit beneath the endothelium and activate the classical pathway, which consumes C4 and C3. Low C3 and C4 with a rising anti-dsDNA titer signal active disease, and both are followed during treatment. Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for lupus and is closely linked to renal involvement.
whyNot: Correct.
Low C3 with normal C4 points to alternative pathway activation, as in poststreptococcal or C3 glomerulopathy.
Normal complement would be unusual with active diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis and its heavy immune complex load.
A normal anti-dsDNA with isolated low C4 does not fit an active lupus flare and suggests problems such as C1 inhibitor deficiency or cryoglobulinemia.

topics: Complement and anti-dsDNA in lupus nephritis

questions.stem: The wire-loop lesions are formed by immune deposits between the capillary endothelium and the glomerular basement membrane. Which feature of this location best explains why these deposits cause intense glomerular inflammation?
options: Separation from blood by the basement membrane
Direct contact with slit diaphragm proteins of podocytes
Location within the mesangial matrix
Contact with blood through endothelial fenestrae
approach: The filtration barrier has three layers from the blood side outward: fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, and podocyte foot processes.
Subendothelial deposits sit on the blood side of the basement membrane, behind only a thin endothelium with open pores.
Complement fragments made there reach the blood, and circulating leukocytes can reach the deposits, so inflammation and proliferation follow.
questions.why: Where an immune deposit sits in the barrier shapes the disease. Subendothelial deposits are separated from the capillary lumen only by fenestrated endothelium. Chemotactic complement fragments such as C5a diffuse into the blood, and neutrophils and monocytes can reach the deposits, so the result is a proliferative, nephritic lesion. Subepithelial deposits lie outside the basement membrane, away from circulating leukocytes, so they mainly injure podocytes and cause nephrotic syndrome, as in membranous nephropathy.
whyNot: Deposits separated from blood by the basement membrane are subepithelial. That position shields them from leukocytes and gives a less inflammatory, nephrotic picture.
The slit diaphragms lie on the urinary side of the basement membrane. Subendothelial deposits do not touch them.
Mesangial deposits are a separate site, typical of IgA nephropathy and milder lupus classes.
Correct.

topics: Layers of the glomerular filtration barrier

questions.stem: Her edema results from renal sodium retention. Her serum sodium concentration is 139 mEq/L (136 to 145). Compared with before her illness, which of the following best describes her body fluid compartments?
options: ECF increased, ICF increased, osmolality decreased
ECF increased, ICF unchanged, osmolality unchanged
ECF increased, ICF decreased, osmolality increased
ECF unchanged, ICF increased, osmolality decreased
approach: A normal serum sodium means the fluid she gained has the same osmolality as plasma, so this is an isotonic gain.
Sodium stays mostly in the extracellular fluid, so isotonic fluid expands only the extracellular compartment.
No osmotic gradient forms, so water does not move into or out of cells.
questions.why: Sodium is the main extracellular solute, so retained sodium with an equal share of water adds isotonic fluid to the extracellular space. Plasma and interstitial volume increase, and the interstitial excess shows as edema. Osmolality is unchanged, so intracellular volume stays the same. A hypotonic gain would swell cells, and a hypertonic gain would shrink them.
whyNot: This is hypotonic fluid gain, as in excess water intake or SIADH, which would lower serum sodium.
Correct.
This is hypertonic gain, as after a hypertonic saline infusion, which would raise serum sodium.
Expansion of cells alone with an unchanged extracellular volume does not fit sodium retention with edema.

topics: Isotonic, hypotonic, and hypertonic volume changes

dx: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis with hepatitis C cryoglobulinemia
case: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of swelling of his legs, a rash on his shins, joint aches, and fatigue for 2 months. He has untreated chronic hepatitis C infection acquired through injection drug use 30 years ago. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 164/96 mm Hg. Examination shows palpable purpura on both lower legs and 2+ pitting edema. Laboratory studies show creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3), albumin 2.6 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5), C3 72 mg/dL (90 to 180), C4 4 mg/dL (10 to 40), and a high rheumatoid factor titer. Cryoglobulins are detected. Urinalysis shows 2+ blood and red blood cell casts, and urine protein is 4.1 g/24 h. Diagnosis: membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis from hepatitis C-associated cryoglobulinemia.

questions.stem: A silver stain of the renal biopsy shows double contours of the glomerular capillary walls. Which of the following processes best explains this appearance?
options: Splitting of the GBM from defective type IV collagen
Subepithelial spikes of new matrix around deposits
Fibrin and parietal cells crowding Bowman space
Mesangial interposition with new basement membrane
approach: A double contour, or tram track, on silver stain means there are two basement membrane layers in the capillary wall.
In membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, subendothelial deposits draw mesangial cells and leukocytes into the capillary wall.
The endothelium then lays down new basement membrane over the cells it has taken in, which creates the second layer.
questions.why: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is named for two changes: thickened capillary walls and proliferating mesangial and endothelial cells. Subendothelial immune deposits draw mesangial cell processes in between the endothelium and the original basement membrane. New basement membrane forms on the inner side, so the silver stain shows two parallel lines. The immune complex form is linked to hepatitis B and C, and dense deposit disease is a C3 glomerulopathy linked to C3 nephritic factor.
whyNot: Split and laminated basement membranes from type IV collagen defects are seen in Alport syndrome, on electron microscopy.
Spikes of new basement membrane around subepithelial deposits are the spike-and-dome pattern of membranous nephropathy.
Fibrin and proliferating parietal cells in Bowman space are crescents, the lesion of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the cryoglobulins most likely responsible for his kidney disease?
options: Monoclonal IgG from a clonal plasma cell disorder
Monoclonal IgM rheumatoid factor with polyclonal IgG
Polyclonal IgA1 complexes with a galactose-deficient hinge
IgG antibodies to double-stranded DNA with nucleosomes
approach: Chronic hepatitis C keeps stimulating B cells and can lead to a clonal B-cell population.
This clone often makes an IgM with rheumatoid factor activity, meaning it binds the Fc part of IgG, which explains his high rheumatoid factor.
The IgM and IgG complexes, often with viral particles, precipitate in the cold and deposit in glomeruli and small vessels of the skin.
questions.why: Hepatitis C is the leading cause of mixed cryoglobulinemia. Long-term viral stimulation of B cells produces a monoclonal IgM, usually kappa, with rheumatoid factor activity. This IgM binds polyclonal IgG, often with hepatitis C particles, forming type II mixed cryoglobulins. The complexes cause small vessel vasculitis (palpable purpura, arthralgia) and deposit beneath the endothelium of glomeruli, producing membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Hepatitis B, by contrast, is linked mainly to membranous nephropathy.
whyNot: A lone monoclonal immunoglobulin is type I cryoglobulinemia, seen in multiple myeloma and Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia. It does not explain a high rheumatoid factor.
Correct.
IgA1 complexes with abnormal hinge glycosylation cause IgA nephropathy and IgA vasculitis, which do not lower complement.
Anti-dsDNA immune complexes are the cause of lupus nephritis, not of hepatitis C cryoglobulinemia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his pattern of serum complement levels?
options: Autoantibody stabilizing the alternative pathway C3 convertase
Loss of complement proteins in nephrotic-range proteinuria
Classical pathway activation by circulating immune complexes
Lectin pathway activation by mannose on bacterial walls
approach: His C4 is very low and his C3 is mildly low.
C4 is used only by the classical and lectin pathways, so a deep drop in C4 points to classical activation by antibody-containing complexes.
IgM-IgG cryoglobulins fix C1 strongly and consume C4 more than C3.
questions.why: Complement levels show which pathway is being used up. The classical pathway starts when C1q binds antibody in immune complexes, then cleaves C4 and C2 before C3. Cryoglobulins with IgM are strong C1 activators, so C4 falls very low while C3 is normal or mildly low. Alternative pathway disease, such as C3 nephritic factor in dense deposit disease or poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, lowers C3 with a normal C4.
whyNot: C3 nephritic factor stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase in dense deposit disease. It lowers C3 but leaves C4 normal.
Urinary loss in nephrotic syndrome does not explain such a marked and selective fall in C4, and his proteinuria is only modestly above 3.5 g/day.
Correct.
Lectin pathway activation by microbial sugars does not fit chronic hepatitis C with circulating cryoglobulins and rheumatoid factor.

questions.stem: Considered alone, which of the following best describes the effect of his low serum albumin on glomerular filtration?
options: Lower glomerular capillary oncotic pressure, favoring filtration
Higher Bowman space hydrostatic pressure, opposing filtration
Lower glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure, opposing filtration
Higher glomerular capillary oncotic pressure, opposing filtration
approach: GFR depends on the filtration coefficient times net filtration pressure: glomerular hydrostatic pressure minus Bowman space hydrostatic pressure minus glomerular oncotic pressure.
Plasma albumin provides most of the oncotic pressure in the glomerular capillary.
Less albumin means less oncotic pressure pulling fluid back, so net filtration pressure rises.
questions.why: Net filtration pressure equals glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure minus Bowman space hydrostatic pressure minus glomerular capillary oncotic pressure. Hypoalbuminemia lowers the oncotic term, which by itself favors filtration. Ureteral obstruction works the other way by raising Bowman space pressure, and dehydration raises oncotic pressure, so both lower GFR. In this patient the GFR is still reduced because proliferation and deposits lower the filtration coefficient, which outweighs the oncotic effect.
whyNot: Correct.
Higher Bowman space pressure is the effect of urinary tract obstruction, not of low albumin.
Lower capillary hydrostatic pressure follows afferent arteriolar constriction or hypotension. Albumin does not set hydrostatic pressure.
Oncotic pressure rises when albumin is concentrated, as in dehydration. Low albumin lowers it.

case: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a rash on her buttocks and legs for 4 days, cramping abdominal pain, and painful swollen ankles. Two weeks ago she had a cough and runny nose. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Examination shows raised purpuric lesions over the buttocks and the backs of the legs, diffuse abdominal tenderness, and swelling and tenderness of both ankles. Laboratory studies show platelet count 310,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000), normal prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times, and creatinine 0.5 mg/dL (0.3 to 0.7). Urinalysis shows 2+ blood, 1+ protein, and red blood cell casts. A stool test for occult blood is positive. Diagnosis: IgA vasculitis with nephritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her skin lesions?
options: IgA immune complexes in small-vessel walls
Autoantibodies against platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa
Consumption of clotting factors in microthrombi
Toxin-mediated endothelial injury with platelet thrombi
approach: Purpura with a normal platelet count and normal clotting times points to a problem in the vessel wall.
Raised (palpable) purpura means inflammation of small vessels, called leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
In a child after an upper respiratory infection, with arthritis, abdominal pain, and nephritis, the cause is IgA immune complex deposition.
questions.why: IgA vasculitis is the most common systemic vasculitis of childhood. After an upper respiratory infection, IgA1-containing immune complexes deposit in the walls of small vessels in the skin, gut, joints, and glomeruli. Complement activation and neutrophil influx damage the vessels, and red cells leak out, so the purpura can be felt. Gut involvement causes colicky pain and bleeding and can lead to intussusception, and the kidney lesion is a mesangial IgA glomerulonephritis.
whyNot: Correct.
Antiplatelet antibodies cause immune thrombocytopenia, which gives flat petechiae with a low platelet count.
Consumption of clotting factors is disseminated intravascular coagulation, which prolongs PT and PTT and lowers platelets.
Shiga toxin endothelial injury is hemolytic uremic syndrome, which causes thrombocytopenia and hemolytic anemia.

questions.stem: Two days later, her abdominal pain becomes severe and intermittent, she vomits, and she passes a stool with blood and mucus. Ultrasonography shows an ileoileal intussusception. Which of the following best explains this complication?
options: Absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon
Hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus
Submucosal hemorrhage and edema as a lead point
Embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery
approach: IgA vasculitis affects small vessels of the bowel wall as well as the skin.
Bleeding and swelling in the submucosa create a mass that peristalsis pulls forward.
The mass acts as a lead point, and the bowel telescopes into the segment below it.
questions.why: IgA immune complexes deposit in small vessels of the gut wall, causing vasculitis with submucosal hemorrhage and edema. This explains her colicky pain and occult blood. A swollen, hemorrhagic segment can act as a lead point that is pulled into the next segment of bowel. In IgA vasculitis the intussusception is often confined to the small bowel, while idiopathic intussusception in infants is usually ileocolic. Intussusception is the most important gastrointestinal complication of IgA vasculitis.
whyNot: Absent ganglion cells in the distal colon is Hirschsprung disease, which presents in the newborn with delayed passage of meconium and constipation.
Pyloric muscle hypertrophy is pyloric stenosis, which causes nonbilious projectile vomiting in the first weeks of life.
Correct.
Superior mesenteric artery embolism causes acute mesenteric ischemia, usually in older adults with atrial fibrillation. It does not telescope the bowel.

questions.stem: A renal biopsy is performed. Which of the following immunofluorescence findings is most likely, and would distinguish her renal lesion from poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
options: Granular C3 along capillary loops
Dominant or codominant mesangial IgA
Linear IgG along the basement membrane
Granular IgG in a starry-sky pattern
approach: IgA vasculitis and IgA nephropathy share the same kidney lesion, mesangial IgA deposits.
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis shows granular IgG and C3, with subepithelial humps.
Pick the finding present in her disease and absent in poststreptococcal disease.
questions.why: The renal lesion of IgA vasculitis looks like IgA nephropathy: mesangial proliferation with IgA as the dominant or codominant immunoglobulin in the mesangium, often with C3. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis shows granular IgG and C3 along capillary walls and subepithelial humps. Timing also helps: her nephritis appeared with the rash, while poststreptococcal disease follows a latent period of weeks and lowers C3.
whyNot: C3 staining can appear in both diseases, so it does not separate them.
Correct.
Linear IgG is anti-GBM disease, which does not fit a child with purpura and arthritis.
Granular IgG in a starry-sky pattern is a pattern of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: Her glomerular IgA deposits lodge in the mesangium, and the mesangial cells proliferate in response. Which of the following is a normal function of these cells?
options: Secretion of renin in response to low perfusion pressure
Detection of sodium chloride delivery to the distal tubule
Production of erythropoietin in response to hypoxia
Uptake and removal of trapped macromolecules
approach: Intraglomerular mesangial cells sit between the capillary loops inside the glomerulus.
They support the loops, can contract, make matrix, and take up macromolecules and immune complexes caught in the filtration barrier.
This clearing role is why circulating complexes, such as IgA complexes, collect in the mesangium and trigger proliferation.
questions.why: Intraglomerular mesangial cells support the capillary tuft, contract to adjust the filtration surface area, make mesangial matrix, and phagocytose macromolecules trapped in the filtration barrier. Because they clear filtered complexes, the mesangium is a common site for immune deposits. IgA complexes that lodge there stimulate the cells to proliferate and release cytokines. Mesangial cells outside the glomerulus (extraglomerular, or lacis, cells) form part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
whyNot: Renin is secreted by juxtaglomerular cells, which are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole.
The macula densa, in the distal thick ascending limb, senses sodium chloride delivery and signals the afferent arteriole and juxtaglomerular cells.
Erythropoietin is made by peritubular interstitial cells of the renal cortex in response to low oxygen delivery.
Correct.

case: A 16-year-old boy is referred because of microscopic hematuria first found at age 6 and recent trouble hearing in class. His mother has had microscopic hematuria with normal kidney function for years. Her brother began dialysis at age 30 and wears hearing aids. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg. Audiometry shows bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Slit-lamp examination shows anterior lenticonus. Urinalysis shows 2+ blood, 2+ protein, and dysmorphic red blood cells. Serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.2). Electron microscopy of a renal biopsy specimen shows irregular thinning, thickening, and splitting of the glomerular basement membrane with a basket-weave appearance. Diagnosis: X-linked Alport syndrome.

questions.stem: A 24-hour urine collection has a volume of 1440 mL and a creatinine concentration of 100 mg/dL. His plasma creatinine concentration that day is 1.6 mg/dL. Which of the following is closest to his creatinine clearance?
options: 63 mL/min
90 mL/min
100 mL/min
160 mL/min
approach: Convert the urine flow: 1440 mL over 1440 minutes is 1.0 mL/min.
Clearance equals urine concentration times urine flow divided by plasma concentration: 100 x 1.0 / 1.6.
The result is about 63 mL/min, a clear fall from a normal value of about 90 to 120 mL/min.
questions.why: Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared of a substance per minute, calculated as U times V divided by P. Creatinine is freely filtered and only slightly secreted, so its clearance approximates GFR. Because a small amount is secreted by the proximal tubule, creatinine clearance slightly overestimates the true GFR. Inulin is filtered and neither secreted nor reabsorbed, so its clearance equals GFR exactly. A substance with clearance below GFR is reabsorbed on balance, and one with clearance above GFR is secreted.
whyNot: Correct.
This value uses 1.44, the daily volume in liters, as if it were the flow in mL/min. Convert first: 1440 mL over 1440 minutes is 1.0 mL/min.
This value is U times V without dividing by plasma creatinine.
This value comes from multiplying by plasma creatinine instead of dividing by it.

questions.stem: In a healthy glomerulus, negatively charged albumin is filtered far less than a neutral dextran molecule of the same size. Which of the following structures is chiefly responsible for this difference?
options: Open fenestrae of the glomerular capillary endothelium
Nephrin bridging the podocyte filtration slit diaphragm
Contractile mesangial cells between capillary loops
Heparan sulfate proteoglycans in the basement membrane
approach: Two molecules of the same size are filtered differently, so the difference is due to charge, not size.
The filtration barrier carries fixed negative charges that repel anionic proteins such as albumin.
The best-known source of these charges is heparan sulfate proteoglycan in the basement membrane.
questions.why: The glomerular filtration barrier has three layers: fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, and podocyte foot processes joined by slit diaphragms. Size selectivity comes mainly from the basement membrane mesh and the slit diaphragm. Charge selectivity comes from negatively charged heparan sulfate proteoglycans in the basement membrane and from the anionic coat on endothelial and podocyte surfaces. Loss of these charges, or loss of foot processes, lets albumin through and causes albuminuria.
whyNot: Endothelial fenestrae are about 70 to 100 nm wide, far larger than albumin, so they do not hold it back by size and the open pores themselves do not repel it.
Nephrin forms the slit diaphragm, which acts mainly as a size barrier. It does not explain a difference between molecules of the same size.
Mesangial cells support the capillary loops and can contract to change surface area, but they do not form part of the filtration barrier.
Correct.

topics: Size and charge selectivity of the filtration barrier

questions.stem: Which of the following genes and inheritance patterns best explain this family's disease?
options: COL4A5, X-linked
COL4A3, autosomal recessive
COL1A1, autosomal dominant
PKD1, autosomal dominant
approach: Hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss, anterior lenticonus, and a split basement membrane identify Alport syndrome, a type IV collagen disorder.
Severe disease in a boy and his maternal uncle, with only mild disease in his mother, fits X-linked inheritance through a carrier mother.
X-linked Alport syndrome, about 80% of cases, is caused by COL4A5 mutations.
questions.why: Alport syndrome is caused by mutations in the genes for the alpha-3, alpha-4, or alpha-5 chains of type IV collagen. These chains form the network of the mature glomerular basement membrane, the cochlea, and the lens capsule, which explains the kidney, ear, and eye findings. About 80% of cases are X-linked, from COL4A5 mutations. The rest are mostly autosomal recessive, from mutations in both copies of COL4A3 or COL4A4, which would rarely give an affected uncle and nephew linked through the mother.
whyNot: Correct.
Autosomal recessive Alport syndrome affects males and females equally and needs mutations from both parents. The pattern through the maternal line points to X-linked disease.
COL1A1 mutations cause osteogenesis imperfecta, with bone fragility and blue sclerae, and do not cause nephritis.
PKD1 mutations cause autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, with enlarged cystic kidneys and no hearing or lens changes.

questions.stem: His 13-year-old sister has persistent microscopic hematuria, normal hearing, and normal kidney function. Genetic testing shows she carries the same mutation. Which of the following best explains her milder disease?
options: Reduced penetrance of an autosomal dominant allele
Maternal uniparental disomy of the X chromosome
Random inactivation of one X in each cell
Anticipation from trinucleotide repeat expansion
approach: The mutation is X-linked, so a male with one mutant X has no normal copy, while a female has a second, normal X.
Early in development each female cell silences one X at random (lyonization).
Podocytes that keep the normal X active make normal type IV collagen, so her basement membrane is partly normal and her disease is milder.
questions.why: Males with X-linked Alport syndrome usually develop progressive renal failure, often by early adulthood, along with hearing loss and eye changes. Heterozygous females are a mosaic because each cell inactivates one X chromosome at random. The share of podocytes expressing the normal allele sets disease severity. Most carrier females have only hematuria, though skewed X inactivation can cause proteinuria and kidney failure later in life.
whyNot: The disease in this family is X-linked, not autosomal dominant, and reduced penetrance does not explain the consistent sex difference.
Maternal uniparental disomy would give her two copies of her mother's X chromosome. That would not make a carrier milder.
Correct.
Anticipation from repeat expansion occurs in disorders such as Huntington disease and myotonic dystrophy, not in collagen point mutations.

case: A 58-year-old woman with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension comes to the physician because of swelling of her legs for 2 months. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 152/90 mm Hg. Funduscopic examination shows dot-blot hemorrhages and hard exudates. There is 2+ pitting edema of the legs. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin A1c 9.1% (4.0 to 5.6), creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), estimated GFR 23 mL/min/1.73 m2 (over 90), and urine protein 4.2 g/24 h. A renal biopsy shows diffuse mesangial expansion with nodular PAS-positive mesangial lesions, thickened glomerular basement membranes, and hyaline arteriolosclerosis of afferent and efferent arterioles. Diagnosis: diabetic nephropathy.

questions.stem: Which of the following processes contributes most directly to the basement membrane thickening and hyaline arteriolar changes in this patient?
options: Deposition of fibrils of misfolded light chains
Granular deposition of circulating immune complexes
Nonenzymatic glycation of matrix proteins
Glycogen accumulation in proximal tubular cells
approach: Years of high glucose let glucose attach to proteins without enzymes, forming Amadori products and then advanced glycation end products (AGEs).
AGEs cross-link collagen and other matrix proteins and trap plasma proteins, so basement membranes thicken and hyaline builds up in arteriolar walls.
Pick nonenzymatic glycation and reject amyloid and immune complex mechanisms.
questions.why: In chronic hyperglycemia, glucose binds the amino groups of long-lived proteins without an enzyme. After rearrangement these become advanced glycation end products. AGEs cross-link type IV collagen and other matrix proteins, trap leaked plasma proteins, and act on the receptor for AGEs (RAGE) to promote fibrosis. The results are basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion with Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules, and hyaline arteriolosclerosis. Early hyperfiltration adds to the injury, and disease moves from microalbuminuria to nephrotic proteinuria and renal failure.
whyNot: Misfolded light chain fibrils are AL amyloid, which forms Congo red-positive deposits and can mimic nodules, but the cause here is diabetes.
Granular immune complexes cause immune complex glomerulonephritis. Diabetic nephropathy has no immune deposits, though IgG and albumin can stick along the membranes.
Correct.
Glycogen in tubular cells (Armanni-Ebstein change) is a real diabetic finding, but it affects tubules and does not thicken basement membranes or arterioles.

questions.stem: As her kidney function declines further, which of the following sets of serum findings is most likely to develop?
options: High phosphate, low calcium, high PTH
Low phosphate, high calcium, low PTH
Low phosphate, low calcium, low PTH
High phosphate, high calcium, low PTH
approach: Falling GFR means less phosphate is excreted, so serum phosphate rises.
Damaged kidneys make less calcitriol, so the gut absorbs less calcium, and phosphate also binds calcium, so serum calcium falls.
Low calcium, high phosphate, and low calcitriol all stimulate the parathyroid glands, causing secondary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.why: Chronic kidney disease, led by diabetes and hypertension, causes a mineral and bone disorder. Phosphate is retained, FGF23 rises, and the renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase falls, so calcitriol drops. Less calcitriol means less intestinal calcium absorption and weaker suppression of PTH. Secondary hyperparathyroidism follows and produces renal osteodystrophy, including high-turnover bone disease. Other consequences of advanced disease include hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia from low erythropoietin, volume overload, and uremic pericarditis and encephalopathy.
whyNot: Correct.
Low phosphate, high calcium, and low PTH would suggest non-PTH hypercalcemia, such as vitamin D excess or malignancy, not kidney failure.
Low phosphate with low calcium and low PTH does not fit a kidney that cannot excrete phosphate.
High calcium with low PTH is uncommon in untreated chronic kidney disease and would suggest excess calcium or vitamin D intake.

topics: Mineral and bone disorder of chronic kidney disease

questions.stem: Two years earlier, when albuminuria was first found, she was started on lisinopril. Shortly after starting the drug, which of the following changes in renal plasma flow (RPF), glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and filtration fraction (FF) would be expected?
options: Increased RPF, increased GFR, increased FF
Decreased RPF, decreased GFR, unchanged FF
Decreased RPF, increased GFR, increased FF
Increased RPF, decreased GFR, decreased FF
approach: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole more than the afferent, so an ACE inhibitor mainly dilates the efferent arteriole.
Less resistance downstream raises flow through the glomerulus but lowers glomerular capillary pressure.
RPF rises, GFR falls, and filtration fraction (GFR divided by RPF) falls.
questions.why: Glomerular pressure depends on the balance of afferent and efferent arteriolar resistance. Efferent dilation lowers total resistance, so renal plasma flow rises, but it also lets pressure drain out of the glomerulus, so GFR falls and filtration fraction falls. In diabetic nephropathy this lower intraglomerular pressure reduces hyperfiltration injury and proteinuria, which is why ACE inhibitors slow progression. A small early rise in creatinine is expected.
whyNot: This pattern does not fit the drug. Efferent dilation lowers glomerular pressure, so GFR and FF fall instead of rising.
Afferent constriction, as from NSAIDs blocking prostaglandins or sympathetic stimulation, lowers both RPF and GFR, leaving FF about the same.
Efferent constriction, as from angiotensin II, lowers RPF but raises GFR and FF. An ACE inhibitor has the opposite effect.
Correct.

topics: Afferent and efferent arteriolar effects on GFR

questions.stem: Ten years ago, before she had kidney disease, she had polyuria and thirst. At that time her plasma glucose was 290 mg/dL (70 to 99 fasting) and her urine glucose was 3+. Which of the following best explains the glucose in her urine at that time?
options: Increased filtration of glucose through a damaged glomerular barrier
Saturation of proximal tubular sodium-glucose cotransport
Active secretion of glucose by collecting duct principal cells
Reduced glucose reabsorption in the thick ascending limb
approach: Glucose is freely filtered, so its filtered load rises in step with plasma glucose.
The proximal tubule reabsorbs glucose through SGLT2 and SGLT1, which have a transport maximum.
Once plasma glucose passes about 200 mg/dL, some nephrons are saturated and glucose spills into the urine, pulling water with it.
questions.why: Filtered glucose is almost all reclaimed in the proximal tubule. SGLT2 in the early segment does most of the work, using the sodium gradient set up by the basolateral Na-K ATPase, and glucose leaves the cell through GLUT2. The carriers have a transport maximum. Glucose first appears in urine at about 200 mg/dL (the renal threshold), because nephrons differ in capacity. Unreabsorbed glucose acts as an osmotic diuretic and causes polyuria and thirst. SGLT2 inhibitor drugs work by producing this glucosuria on purpose.
whyNot: Glucose is freely filtered by a normal glomerulus, so barrier damage does not increase its filtration.
Correct.
The collecting duct does not secrete glucose. Glucose is handled by filtration and proximal reabsorption only.
The thick ascending limb reabsorbs sodium, potassium, and chloride through NKCC2 and has no role in glucose reabsorption.

topics: Renal glucose handling and transport maximum

case: A 38-year-old Black man comes to the physician because of leg swelling and foamy urine for 1 month. HIV infection was diagnosed 6 months ago, and he has not started antiretroviral therapy. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. There is 3+ pitting edema of the legs. Laboratory studies show CD4+ T-lymphocyte count 180/mm3 (500 to 1500), albumin 2.2 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5), total cholesterol 310 mg/dL (under 200), and creatinine 2.8 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Urine protein is 9.8 g/24 h. Ultrasonography shows enlarged, echogenic kidneys. A renal biopsy shows collapse of glomerular capillary tufts with enlarged overlying podocytes, dilated tubules, and no immune deposits on immunofluorescence. Diagnosis: HIV-associated nephropathy (collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis).

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is also a recognized secondary cause of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis?
options: Hodgkin lymphoma
Chronic hepatitis B infection
Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis
Sickle cell disease
approach: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is a podocyte injury that leaves scars in parts of some glomeruli.
Secondary causes either injure podocytes directly (HIV, heroin) or overload the remaining nephrons through hyperfiltration (sickle cell disease, obesity, reduced nephron mass).
Match each option to the glomerular disease it is classically linked with.
questions.why: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, especially Black adults, and it responds poorly to corticosteroids. Secondary causes include HIV infection, heroin use, sickle cell disease, obesity, and loss of nephron mass. In sickle cell disease, chronic anemia and hyperfiltration strain the podocytes. The collapsing variant, typical of HIV, has the worst prognosis and progresses quickly to renal failure.
whyNot: Hodgkin lymphoma is linked to minimal change disease, likely through T cell cytokines that injure podocytes.
Chronic hepatitis B is linked mainly to membranous nephropathy and also to membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
Long-standing inflammatory disease such as rheumatoid arthritis causes AA amyloidosis, which deposits Congo red-positive fibrils in glomeruli.
Correct.

topics: Secondary causes of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Glomerular diseases linked to systemic conditions

questions.stem: Urine sediment examined under polarized light shows round bodies with a Maltese cross pattern. These structures are most likely composed of which of the following?
options: Calcium oxalate monohydrate crystals from oxalate excess
Cholesterol esters in lipid-laden tubular cells
Uric acid crystals in acidic urine
Myoglobin pigment within coarse granular casts
approach: Heavy proteinuria and a high cholesterol mean nephrotic syndrome.
In nephrotic syndrome the liver makes more lipoproteins and their breakdown slows, and lipoproteins leak through the damaged barrier.
Tubular cells take up the filtered lipid and are shed as oval fat bodies, whose cholesterol esters show a Maltese cross under polarized light.
questions.why: Low oncotic pressure in nephrotic syndrome stimulates hepatic synthesis of lipoproteins, including LDL and lipoprotein(a). Lipoprotein lipase activity falls, so VLDL breakdown also slows, and cholesterol and triglycerides rise. Lipoproteins that cross the injured barrier are taken up by tubular cells. These cells shed into the urine as oval fat bodies, or the lipid is trapped in fatty casts. Cholesterol esters are birefringent and show a Maltese cross under polarized light.
whyNot: Calcium oxalate monohydrate crystals are dumbbell or needle shaped, as in ethylene glycol poisoning. They do not form Maltese crosses.
Correct.
Uric acid crystals are yellow rhomboid or rosette shaped. They form in acidic urine, as in gout and tumor lysis.
Myoglobin pigment gives dark granular casts in rhabdomyolysis and does not show a Maltese cross.

topics: Oval fat bodies and fatty casts

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms best explains this patient's kidney injury?
options: Viral gene expression in infected podocytes
Granular immune complexes of HIV antigens
Proximal tubule toxicity of antiretroviral drugs
Opportunistic cytomegalovirus infection of glomeruli
approach: Collapsing glomerulosclerosis with enlarged podocytes and no immune deposits means the podocytes are injured directly.
HIV infects podocytes and tubular epithelial cells, and viral proteins such as Nef and Vpr make podocytes lose their mature features and proliferate.
Untreated infection with a falling CD4 count and inherited APOL1 risk variants raise the risk.
questions.why: HIV-associated nephropathy is caused by direct infection of renal epithelial cells. HIV genes expressed in podocytes, especially nef and vpr, make the cells lose their mature features and proliferate, so the capillary tuft collapses. Infected tubular cells cause microcystic tubular dilation, which helps make the kidneys large and echogenic. The disease is far more common in people of African ancestry who carry two APOL1 risk variants. Antiretroviral therapy reduces the risk and slows progression.
whyNot: Correct.
HIV immune complex kidney disease exists, but it shows granular deposits on immunofluorescence. His biopsy shows none.
Drugs such as tenofovir can injure the proximal tubule, but he has not started antiretroviral therapy, and tubular injury does not cause nephrotic-range proteinuria.
Cytomegalovirus infection occurs at very low CD4 counts and causes retinitis, colitis, and pneumonitis. It does not cause collapsing glomerulosclerosis.

questions.stem: Three weeks later, he develops sudden left flank pain and gross hematuria. Doppler ultrasonography shows thrombosis of the left renal vein. He has not received heparin. Which of the following most likely contributed to this complication?
options: Antibodies to heparin and platelet factor 4
Decreased hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen
Urinary loss of antithrombin III
Reduced plasma factor VIII activity
approach: Nephrotic syndrome is a hypercoagulable state, and renal vein thrombosis is a classic complication.
Antithrombin III is a midsize protein that leaks through the damaged barrier, while large clotting factors stay in the blood and rise with increased hepatic synthesis.
Losing a natural anticoagulant while procoagulants rise tips the balance toward clotting.
questions.why: Nephrotic syndrome changes several systems at once. Albumin loss lowers oncotic pressure and causes edema. The liver responds by making more proteins, including lipoproteins, fibrinogen, and factors V and VIII, so lipids and procoagulants rise. Antithrombin III, about the size of albumin, is lost in the urine, which removes a key brake on thrombin and factor Xa. Renal vein thrombosis is the classic result, and it is most common in membranous nephropathy. Loss of immunoglobulins also raises the risk of infection.
whyNot: Heparin-PF4 antibodies cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which needs prior heparin exposure. He has not received heparin.
Fibrinogen synthesis increases in nephrotic syndrome. Less fibrinogen would reduce clotting.
Correct.
Factor VIII is a large protein that is kept in the blood and rises in nephrotic syndrome. Low factor VIII would cause bleeding.
